title: EV charger access, Galway City
text:
QuestionHow far, by road, does each Galway City resident live from an EV charger?
  ToolsQGIS (QuickOSM, QNEAT3), PyQGIS
  Data28 EV chargers from OpenStreetMap; 309 CSO Census 2022 Small Areas with population; OpenStreetMap road network
  CRSIrish Transverse Mercator (EPSG:2157)

title: EV charger access, Galway City
text:
Problem
Ireland’s EV targets depend on people being able to charge, but straight-line distance hides how far people actually have to drive. This project measures road distance from every Census Small Area in Galway City to its nearest charger, then weights the result by population to show how many residents are poorly served.

title: EV charger access, Galway City
text:
Data

28 EV charger locations from OpenStreetMap, downloaded with QuickOSM
309 CSO Census 2022 Small Area boundaries, joined to Small Area Population Statistics
OpenStreetMap road network for Galway City

title: EV charger access, Galway City
text:
Method

Reprojected every layer to Irish Transverse Mercator so all distances are in metres
Created a centroid for each Small Area
Measured straight-line distance to the nearest charger (Distance to Nearest Hub)
Measured road-network distance with a QNEAT3 origin–destination matrix, keeping the shortest route for each Small Area
Joined Census population to turn distances into numbers of residents
Built the A4 layout with a PyQGIS script, so the headline figures are calculated from the data rather than typed in

title: EV charger access, Galway City
text:
Result



Road distance to the nearest EV charger by Census Small Area, with the 10 furthest and 10 nearest areas outlined. Inset: the same classes using straight-line distance.



66% of residents (about 55,600 people) live more than 1 km by road from a charger.
28% (23,960 people) live more than 2 km away, and 5% (4,199 people) more than 3 km.
1.5 km is the average resident’s distance to the nearest charger, weighted by population.
Chargers cluster in the city centre, so the outer residential edges of the city are the worst served.
Straight-line distance understates real trips, most of all where the river or the bay forces a detour.

title: EV charger access, Galway City
text:
Limitations

Distances are measured from Small Area centroids, so parts of large Small Areas are closer to a charger than shown.
OpenStreetMap charger data may be incomplete and can include chargers that aren’t open to the public.
One Small Area has no road connection. It is counted in the population total but not in the distance figures.

title: Rainfall interpolation by kriging
text:
QuestionHow can scattered rain gauge readings be turned into a reliable rainfall map, and which kriging method predicts best?
  ToolsR (sf, gstat, terra, mgcv, elevatr), QGIS
  DataMean annual rainfall at 438 rain gauges; CSO 2022 Small Area boundaries; elevation model from elevatr
  CRSIrish Transverse Mercator (EPSG:2157)
  ContextAdvanced GIS module, University of Galway

title: Rainfall interpolation by kriging
text:
Problem
Rainfall is measured at a limited number of rain gauges, but planning, flood risk and environmental work need values everywhere. Kriging predicts values between stations from how similar nearby readings are, and different versions of it handle trends and terrain differently. This project tests four versions against each other and combines them.

title: Rainfall interpolation by kriging
text:
Data

Mean annual rainfall at 438 rain gauges, with station height, reprojected to Irish Transverse Mercator
CSO 2022 Small Area boundaries, merged into a single outline of the Republic of Ireland
A digital elevation model downloaded with elevatr, used as a predictor

title: Rainfall interpolation by kriging
text:
Method

Built a 1 km prediction grid over the Republic of Ireland
Ordinary kriging with a spherical variogram fitted to the station data
Universal kriging with an east–north trend, because rainfall falls steadily towards the east and, to a lesser extent, the north
Universal kriging with elevation added to the trend, because rainfall rises with altitude
Regression kriging: a generalised additive model (GAM) of easting, northing and elevation, with its residuals kriged and added back
Tested every model with cross-validation (100-fold, and leave-one-out for regression kriging) and compared the RMSE
Averaged the four predictions into an ensemble, which had the lowest cross-validation error of all the approaches, and mapped it in QGIS

title: Rainfall interpolation by kriging
text:
Result



Ensemble prediction of mean annual rainfall at 1 km resolution, with the same gauges interpolated by nearest neighbour and inverse distance weighting for comparison. Click to enlarge.



Predicted rainfall ranges from 668 mm to 3,355 mm a year.
The wettest areas are the mountains of west Mayo and Kerry, with a smaller peak over the Wicklow Mountains.
The east and midlands are driest, matching the east–west trend the universal kriging picked up.
Elevation explains most of the local detail. Once east, north and elevation were in the model, the trend accounted for most of the variation, and kriging the residuals added fine-scale correction.
Averaging beat every single model. The ensemble of all four had the lowest cross-validation error.
Kriging with elevation follows the terrain. Nearest neighbour and inverse distance weighting only spread each gauge’s value outwards, so they miss rain on high ground between gauges.

title: Rainfall interpolation by kriging
text:
Limitations

The grid covers the Republic of Ireland only, because the outline comes from CSO Small Areas.
Only 23 of the 438 gauges are above 300 m, and the highest is at 701 m. Rainfall on the highest mountains is extrapolated from the elevation trend rather than measured, so the mountain peaks are the least certain part of the map.
Rainfall is not normally distributed. Log-normal kriging would suit it better but makes back-transforming the predictions much harder.

title: Boston commuter flows
text:
QuestionWhere do people in the Boston metro live, where do they work, and how far do they travel between the two?
  ToolsPython (pandas, NumPy), deck.gl, JavaScript
  DataLEHD LODES8 origin–destination data, 2023, primary jobs; Census 2023 cartographic boundary tracts
  Study areaMassachusetts part of the Boston-Cambridge-Newton metro: 1,028 census tracts, 147 towns

title: Boston commuter flows
text:
Live map
Hover a tract to see where its residents work and where its workers live. Switch between town and tract flows, filter by the number of workers, or click a corridor in the side panel to map it.

  

Open the map full screen

title: Boston commuter flows
text:
Problem
Commuting shapes housing demand, transit planning and traffic, but census tables only give totals. LODES records the home and work location of almost every job in Massachusetts, which makes it possible to map the actual flows between neighbourhoods and measure how far people travel.

title: Boston commuter flows
text:
Data

LEHD LODES8 origin–destination file for Massachusetts, 2023, primary jobs only (JT01), so each worker is counted once
LODES geography crosswalk, linking each census block to its tract, town and metro area
US Census 2023 cartographic boundary tracts, clipped to the shoreline

title: Boston commuter flows
text:
Method

Filtered 1.7 million home-to-work block pairs to those with both ends in the Massachusetts part of the metro
Measured straight-line distance between the home and work block for every pair, then weighted by workers, so short commutes within a tract are not counted as zero
Summed the flows to tract pairs and town pairs, and placed each arc end at the worker-weighted centre of its tract or town, so arcs land where people actually live and work
Mapped the flows as a deck.gl arc layer, with town flows for the overview and tract flows for detail
Read the shapefile directly in Python, with no GDAL dependency, and built the page from a single data file

title: Boston commuter flows
text:
Result

1.88 million workers live and work in the Massachusetts part of the metro.
16.6 km (10.3 miles) is the average commute in a straight line, and the median is 12.3 km.
23% of workers commute less than 5 km, while 32% commute 20 km or more.
21% work in the town they live in. In Boston itself, 58% of residents work in the city, but Boston residents hold only 31% of Boston’s 555,000 jobs.
The busiest corridor is Boston to Cambridge (22,805 workers), followed by Quincy to Boston (18,621) and Cambridge to Boston (18,573).
Higher earners commute farther. Workers earning over $3,333 a month travel 17.3 km on average, against 14.7 km for those earning $1,250 or less.
The Financial District is the largest single job tract, with almost 75,000 jobs.

title: Boston commuter flows
text:
Limitations

Distances are straight-line. Real trips by road or transit are longer.
LODES home locations are partly synthetic to protect privacy, so results are reported at tract and town level, and the map only draws tract pairs with 3 or more workers.
The metro’s two New Hampshire counties are not in the Massachusetts file, so they are left out.

title: Galway urban sprawl, 1990–2025
text:
QuestionHow far and in which direction has Galway grown since 1990, and has planning policy changed that path?
  ToolsQGIS, R
  DataCORINE Land Cover (1990, 2000, 2006, 2012, 2018); four Galway City Development Plans (2005–2029)
  Study area9 km buffer centred on Eyre Square
  CRSIrish Transverse Mercator (EPSG:2157)
  ContextBSc dissertation, University of Galway. Graded 78%.

title: Galway urban sprawl, 1990–2025
text:
Problem
Galway City nearly doubled its urban footprint during the Celtic Tiger years. Each City Development Plan since has promised compact growth, brownfield regeneration and a shift away from car dependency. This project tests whether the city has actually changed course, or whether new sustainability language has been layered on top of the suburban pattern set in the 1990s.

title: Galway urban sprawl, 1990–2025
text:
Data

CORINE Land Cover rasters at five time points, reclassified to urban and non-urban land
Four consecutive Galway City Development Plans, 2005–2011 to 2023–2029

title: Galway urban sprawl, 1990–2025
text:
Method

Clipped each CORINE year to a 9 km buffer around Eyre Square and processed it in QGIS
Measured four things for each year: total urban land, density across concentric rings, fragmentation (patch count and Largest Patch Index) and the area-weighted centroid of urban land
Coded each development plan against ten codes, five path dependency indicators and five transition signals, in two passes for consistency
Compared what the plans promised with what the land cover record shows

title: Galway urban sprawl, 1990–2025
text:
Result



Urban extent by CORINE year. Growth spread west towards Knocknacarra, east along the N6 corridor and out to Oranmore.



88% growth. The urban footprint grew by 88% between 1990 and 2018, and virtually all of it happened before 2006.
Fragmented growth. Fragmentation peaked in 2006 at 32 separate urban patches, with the largest single patch only 29.5% of urban land.
No reversal. After the 2008 crash, growth stopped, but the dispersed pattern it left behind did not reverse.




1990 urban land compared with 2018. Most new land sits on the edges of the city and outside the city boundary.





Movement of the area-weighted centre of urban land between CORINE years.



The centre of growth moved. It shifted 885 m west during the 1990s as suburbs spread towards Knocknacarra. It then swung 1,063 m east by 2006 and 501 m back west by 2012, where it stayed.

title: Galway urban sprawl, 1990–2025
text:
Policy findings

45 coded entries across the four plans: 17 path dependency indicators and 28 transition signals.
More sustainability language. The ratio of path dependency to transition signals fell from 1.20 in the 2005–2011 plan to 0.30 in the 2023–2029 plan.
Same unfinished projects. The ring road, Ardaun new town and Ceannt Quarter regeneration appear in all four plans without being delivered.
Little new governance. Only one entry across all four plans coded as innovative governance.

title: Galway urban sprawl, 1990–2025
text:
Conclusion
Galway’s planning shows layering rather than real transition. Sustainability commitments have grown more ambitious with each plan, but the car-dependent suburban form built in the 1990s is still in place. The 2023–2029 plan, backed by national mandates, gives some grounds for a new path, but the lack of new delivery mechanisms suggests the pattern has not yet broken.

title: Nautical lights of Ireland
text:
QuestionCan open data reproduce what a sailor sees at night: every light on the Irish coast, flashing on its real cycle?
  ToolsPython (requests, NumPy, Pillow), HTML canvas and JavaScript
  DataOpenSeaMap light tags from OpenStreetMap (Overpass API); Terrarium elevation tiles (AWS Terrain Tiles)
  ProjectionWeb Mercator

title: Nautical lights of Ireland
text:
Live map
Hover over a light to see its name, character and range. Every light flashes on its real charted cycle.

  

Open the map full screen

title: Nautical lights of Ireland
text:
Problem
Every lighthouse, beacon and buoy light has a published character, such as Fl(2) W 10s, that tells sailors how it flashes. Lighthouse maps usually show these lights as static dots. This project turns the characters back into motion, so the map shows the coast the way it looks from the sea at night.

title: Nautical lights of Ireland
text:
Data

Every charted light around Ireland with seamark:light tags in OpenStreetMap, fetched through the Overpass API
Terrarium elevation tiles for the hillshade and for blocking beams with terrain

title: Nautical lights of Ireland
text:
Method

Clipped the lights with a polygon to drop Scottish and Welsh lights inside the bounding box
Merged lights within 300 m of each other, keeping the one with the longest range, so harbour clusters don’t blur into one blob
Parsed each light’s character (Fl, Oc, Iso, Q, LFl, Mo and combinations such as VQ(6)+LFl) into an on/off timeline, using the exact sequence tag where it exists
Built a dark hillshade from the elevation tiles with NumPy
Gave rotating beams to lights with a range of 12 nautical miles or more, and ray-cast each beam against the terrain degree by degree, so headlands cut them off
Drew everything on an HTML canvas with additive blending, so overlapping glows merge along the coast
Added a built-in video recorder, which exports a 4:5 clip sized for Instagram

title: Nautical lights of Ireland
text:
Result

449 lights on the Irish coast after merging harbour clusters: 184 white, 146 red, 102 green, 16 yellow and 1 blue.
34 major lights have rotating beams, such as Fastnet Rock, which flashes white every 5 seconds with a range of 28 nautical miles.
Most of the lights are not lighthouses. They are buoys and harbour beacons, which is why the map is titled nautical lights.

title: Nautical lights of Ireland
text:
Limitations

OpenStreetMap is the only openly licensed source of Irish light data, so lights missing from OSM are missing from the map.
Each light is given a random starting point in its cycle, so the timing between neighbouring lights is not real.
